section.title: He Raises the Poor from the Dust
section.sectionRationale: The opening psalm of the Egyptian Hallel, Psalms 113-118, sung at Passover and other great feasts, this hymn celebrates the LORD who is exalted above all nations yet stoops to lift the poor from the dust and give the barren woman a home, the very pattern later sung by Hannah and Mary.
section.thesis: The LORD who is exalted above the heavens stoops to notice the lowest of the earth, raising the poor from the dust and seating them with princes, a downward reach that is itself the shape of the gospel.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a threefold call to praise stretching from sunrise to sunset, verses 1-3; the lofty King who stoops to look upon heaven and earth, verses 4-6; and the LORD who lifts the poor and the barren to honor and joy, verses 7-9.

units.label: Praise from where the sun rises to where it sets
units.note: the call to praise, opening the Hallel

verses.text: Hallelujah! Give praise, O servants of the LORD; praise the name of the LORD.
Blessed be the name of the LORD both now and forevermore.
From where the sun rises to where it sets, the name of the LORD is praised.

units.label: He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth
units.note: the lofty King who stoops low

verses.text: The LORD is exalted over all the nations, His glory above the heavens.
Who is like the LORD our God, the One enthroned on high?
He {{shaphel|humbles Himself}} to behold the heavens and the earth.

units.label: He raises the poor from the dust
units.note: reversal of fortunes, echoed by Hannah and Mary

verses.text: He raises the poor from the {{dal|dust}} and lifts the needy from the dump
to seat them with nobles, with the princes of His people.
He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children. Hallelujah!

shaphel.gloss: To stoop, bring low, humble oneself. The verb pictures God, enthroned high above the heavens, bending down to look at, and act upon, the affairs of heaven and earth, a divine condescension fulfilled supremely in the incarnation.

dal.gloss: Poor, low, weak, powerless. Paired with the needy in verse 7, this describes those with no resources or status of their own, whom the LORD lifts from the dust to seat among princes.

basic.context: This psalm opens the Egyptian Hallel, Psalms 113 through 118, sung by pilgrims at Passover and other feasts, and later by Jesus and His disciples at the Last Supper, Matthew 26:30. It moves from a global summons to praise, to the wonder of God's transcendence, to the still greater wonder of His condescension to the lowly.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's shape, exaltation above the heavens paired with stooping to the dust, teaches that God's greatness is displayed not despite His care for the powerless but precisely in it, a pattern the New Testament identifies as the shape of the gospel itself.
basic.originalLanguages: God is described as shaphel, stooping or humbling Himself, verse 6, to behold heaven and earth, even though He is enthroned on high. He lifts the dal, the poor and powerless, verse 7, from the dust to seat them among princes, a reversal completed in giving the barren woman a home.
basic.typology: This psalm's reversal, God stooping from the heights to lift the lowly, directly anticipates the pattern of Hannah's song, 1 Samuel 2:8, and is echoed almost verbatim in Mary's Magnificat, Luke 1:52-53, both of which find their fulfillment in the incarnation, where the eternal Son stoops from heaven's throne to be born of a woman.
basic.christ: This psalm's picture of the exalted LORD humbling Himself to behold and to lift the lowly is fulfilled supremely in Christ, who, though in the form of God, emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-8. He raises the spiritually poor and needy, seating them with Him in the heavenly realms, Ephesians 2:6, the ultimate answer to this psalm's raising of the poor from the dust.
basic.god: God is at once utterly exalted above every nation and every heaven, and personally near enough to notice, and to reverse, the plight of the poorest and most overlooked person on earth, including the sorrow of the barren woman.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 2:8 supplies nearly identical language of God raising the poor from the dust, part of Hannah's song. Luke 1:52-53, Mary's Magnificat, echoes this same reversal of the humble being exalted. Philippians 2:6-8 shows Christ's own descent from glory as the ultimate fulfillment of God's stooping love.
basic.oneStory: The LORD who is exalted above every nation stoops to lift the poor from the dust and give joy to the barren, a pattern sung by Hannah and by Mary and fulfilled completely in Christ, who emptied Himself from the heights of glory to lift sinners from the dust of death and seat them with Him in the heavenly places.

context.literary:
Psalm 113 is a small hymn with a very clear shape: three verses, three verses, three verses. The first block, verses 1 to 3, is a summons. The word 'praise' comes three times in verse 1 and the name of the LORD is named in each of the first three verses, and the block stretches the praise through time ('now and forevermore,' verse 2) and across space ('from where the sun rises to where it sets,' verse 3). So the opening gathers the whole of time and the whole of the earth around a single name.

The second block, verses 4 to 6, gives the grounds and turns on a question: 'Who is like the LORD our God?' The question is rhetorical, and the answer the psalm gives is surprising. The first answer is the expected one, that He is exalted over all the nations and above the heavens, verse 4. The second is not another description of height but of lowness: He is 'enthroned on high,' and yet He bends down to look. Verses 5 and 6 are built from two matching participles, one for the God who makes Himself high and one for the God who makes Himself low, so the verse holds both movements together in a single breath.

The third block, verses 7 to 9, shows the stooping in action. Two lines are about the poor and needy, and the third is about the barren woman. The same verb for sitting appears across the psalm: God is 'enthroned' in verse 5, He 'seats' the poor with princes in verse 8, and He 'settles' the barren woman in verse 9. The One who sits on the highest throne gives seats to those who had none. The psalm begins and ends with 'Hallelujah,' so that praise bookends the whole, and the movement from the name of the LORD to the home of a childless woman shows how far the stooping reaches.
context.historical:
Psalm 113 opens the group of psalms 113 to 118 that Jewish tradition called the Egyptian Hallel, because Psalm 114 recalls the Exodus. These psalms became the songs of the great feasts, and above all of Passover. As later Jewish sources describe it, Psalms 113 and 114 were sung at the table before the meal and 115 to 118 after it. That is probably what the Gospels have in mind when they say that Jesus and His disciples, having finished the supper, 'sang a hymn' and went out to the Mount of Olives, Matthew 26:30. If so, the song that opened the evening's praise is the one that speaks of God stooping to lift the lowly, sung on the night before the cross.

The people who first sang it knew what it was to be low. Israel's own story began in the dust of slavery in Egypt, and the psalm that follows this one recalls how God brought them out, Psalm 114:1-2. 'Dust' and the 'ash heap' were the places of the destitute and the mourning. Job sat among ashes, Job 2:8, and Lamentations speaks of people 'huddling in ash heaps,' Lamentations 4:5. The lines about sitting with nobles would sound extraordinary to anyone who had known such a place.

The barren woman had a particular burden in Israel. A family's future and a woman's standing in the community depended heavily on children, and barrenness was seen as shame. Rachel said, 'God has taken away my shame,' when she conceived, Genesis 30:23, and Elizabeth said that the Lord 'has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people,' Luke 1:25. The names of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah would have sprung to mind at the end of the psalm. Each of them is a woman whom God settled in a home as a joyful mother.

The call to praise is addressed to 'servants of the LORD,' verse 1. The same address appears in Psalm 134:1 and Psalm 135:1-2, where it refers to those who serve in the house of the LORD, so the summons may have first gone to the worshippers in the temple court, though it is then widened to the whole earth.
context.canonical:
The psalm draws on the prayer of a woman who stood where its last verse stands. Hannah, who was barren and ridiculed, sang after the birth of Samuel that God 'raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes,' 1 Samuel 2:8. Verses 7 and 8 of Psalm 113 are almost the same words, and the barren woman who 'gives birth to seven' in 1 Samuel 2:5 has her echo in verse 9. The psalm turns a single woman's thanksgiving into a hymn for the whole assembly.

The theme of the God who is high and yet near runs through the prophets and the wisdom writers. Psalm 138:6 says, 'Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly.' Isaiah 57:15 has the One who is 'high and lifted up' say, 'I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit.' Isaiah 66:1-2 says that heaven is His throne, and then that the one He esteems is the humble and contrite one who trembles at His word. Job 5:11 declares that 'He sets the lowly on high.' In every case the highness of God is not a barrier but the ground of His care.

The psalm is carried into the New Testament by two women. Mary's Magnificat takes up Hannah's song and Psalm 113 together: 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' Luke 1:52, and 'He has filled the hungry with good things,' Luke 1:53. Zechariah's wife Elizabeth is the barren woman raised to joy, Luke 1:7 and 1:25. Beyond the Gospels, Paul takes up the theme of the barren woman and applies Isaiah 54:1 to the church in Galatians 4:27. And the hymn in Philippians 2:5-11, which tells of the one who stooped and was then exalted to the highest place, is the same shape of story as the psalm, told of the Son of God.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted Israel to recognise that the greatness of their God was of a different kind from the greatness of the powers around them. The surrounding nations imagined gods who were high and remote, served by the strong and the rich. This psalm says that the LORD's height does not keep Him from the poor. The test of His greatness is the question 'Who is like the LORD our God?' and the answer is that no one else is great in both directions, high above the heavens and low enough to see the person on the ash heap.

For a people who had known slavery and dispossession, this was comfort and a standard. It was comfort because God had a track record of lifting up the helpless, and it was a standard because those who bear His name are expected to value what He values. A worshipper who sang that God raises the needy could hardly then despise the needy.

The psalm also means to widen the circle of praise. It begins by calling the servants of the LORD to praise, and then extends the praise 'from where the sun rises to where it sets.' The final scene is small and domestic, a woman in a home with her children, and the psalm wants the first hearers to find the glory of God in places they would not think to look. The author hoped that when they saw an unremarkable woman at home with her children, they would think of the God who is exalted over the nations.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what God does, and it gives only one command, the call to praise in verse 1. There is no instruction to the reader about what to do for the poor. What it does, by showing the character of the God who is worshipped, is to set a direction for the people of that God. The proverb says that kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, Proverbs 19:17, and Jesus tells His disciples that the one who leads should be like the one who serves, Luke 22:26. The psalm supplies the reason behind those commands.

The promise to the barren woman must be read as a description of a pattern in God's dealings and not as a law. The women of Genesis, Judges and Samuel who were given children were real, but so were many faithful women who never bore a child. To treat verse 9 as a promise to every childless believer would be to wound people the psalm does not mean to wound. The better application is that God notices those whom others pass over, and that He knows how to bring joy out of grief. That joy may take forms other than a child, and Scripture itself shows this, for example in the promise to those who are not able to have children in Isaiah 54:1, where the barren woman's family is the people of God.

debates.question: Does verse 6 say that God humbles Himself, or that He looks a long way down?

views.label: God condescends: He lowers Himself to see
views.case: The Hebrew participle is a causative form of the verb for being low, and the BSB follows it with 'humbles Himself.' The verse is set directly against verse 5, where He is 'enthroned on high,' and the pair shows that God is both lofty and willing to bend. The reading fits the way the psalm goes on to the dust and the ash heap and the New Testament use of the pattern in Philippians 2:6-8.

views.label: God looks far down, since even the heavens are beneath Him
views.case: Some translations render the line as 'who looks far down on heaven and earth.' On that reading the verse is about distance, not about willingness. Heaven and earth both lie beneath the One who sits above them, and the point is the scale of His greatness, as in Isaiah 40:22, where He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth.

debates.bearing: Either way, the next verses show Him acting on behalf of the lowly, and the psalm's own movement from height to dust favours the idea of condescension. The two readings are not far apart, since the second only emphasises how much stooping there is to do.

debates.question: Does verse 9 guarantee that every barren woman who trusts God will bear children?

views.label: It is a pattern of God's dealings, illustrated by the matriarchs
views.case: The psalm draws on the stories of Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, Genesis 21:1-2, Genesis 30:22-23 and 1 Samuel 2:5, in which God did give children. It presents these as examples of a God who reverses hopeless situations, not as a promise to every individual.

views.label: It points beyond childbirth to God's power to bring fruitfulness from any barrenness
views.case: The psalm sets the barren woman beside the poor lifted from the dust, both pictures of reversal. Isaiah 54:1 and Galatians 4:27 apply the picture of the barren woman to the people of God as a whole, so its scope is wider than the womb.

debates.bearing: The psalm affirms that God sees the childless and brings joy where there was shame, and it does not promise a particular outcome to every person. The pastoral use of the verse should be gentle and should lean on the God who notices and not on a guaranteed result.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm calls God's people to praise His 'name,' shem, and the name is the only thing the first three verses name. In the Old Testament a name is a person's character and reputation made known, so to praise the name is to praise what God has shown Himself to be. The summons runs from 'now and forevermore' and from the rising to the setting of the sun, a pairing that Malachi 1:11 also uses of the name of the LORD being great among the nations.

The question of verse 5, 'Who is like the LORD our God?' is a question in Hebrew that sounds like a name. The prophet Micah's name means 'who is like the LORD,' and Micah 7:18 asks, 'Who is a God like You?' The form echoes the song of Moses, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?' Exodus 15:11. The question is a standard confession of Israel's faith, a rhetorical claim that there is no rival.

The two participles of verses 5 and 6 are both causative forms. The first describes the God who 'makes high to sit,' and the second describes the God who 'makes low to see.' The BSB renders the first as 'enthroned on high' and the second as 'humbles Himself,' reading the causative as something God does to Himself. It is worth noticing that the grammar sets the two side by side, with no word like 'but' to separate them, so the height and the lowness are one description of the same God.

The word 'poor,' dal, in verse 7 means someone who is weak, low or without resources, the kind of person who is easily pushed aside. It stands beside 'needy,' evyon, the one who is in want. Both words are common in the Psalms and the Prophets, and they often name those whom God defends. The 'dust' is aphar, the stuff from which humans were made in Genesis 2:7 and to which they return in Genesis 3:19, so to be lifted from the dust is to be lifted from the place of death. The 'ash heap,' ashpot, which the BSB renders 'dump,' is the heap of refuse and ashes outside the town where the destitute might lie. The verse is word for word the same as the one in Hannah's song, 1 Samuel 2:8.

In verse 8 the poor are seated 'with nobles,' nedivim, a word that can also mean willing or generous, from the root nadav. The nobles are the generous ones, and the word is the same root as the 'willing' people of Psalm 110:3. The line adds that the poor sit with 'the nobles of His people,' so they are not given a separate or lesser place but are seated at the same table.

The verb for sitting, yashav, runs through the psalm. God is the one who sits on high in verse 5, He causes the poor to sit with nobles in verse 8, and He 'settles' the barren woman in verse 9. The Hebrew phrase for her is closer to 'the barren one of the house,' so the woman had been a childless presence in her own home, and God turns her into 'a joyful mother of children.' The joy is placed at the very end, just before the final Hallelujah.

typology.type: The poor raised from the dust to sit with princes, verses 7 and 8
typology.fulfillment: Scripture gives several living pictures of this reversal. Joseph is brought out of the dungeon and placed over all Egypt, with men calling out 'Bow the knee,' Genesis 41:14, 41-43. David is taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd God's people, Psalm 78:70-71. In each case a lowly person is lifted by God to a place beside the powerful. The escalation comes in Christ, who was laid in the 'dust of death,' Psalm 22:15, and raised to God's right hand, and who then raises His people: God 'raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms,' Ephesians 2:6. The earlier examples fall short because they raised individuals to earthly places, and none of them could lift others out of death.

typology.type: The barren woman made a joyful mother, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: Sarah, Rachel, Hannah, Manoah's wife and Elizabeth form a line of women whose barrenness is turned to joy by God, Genesis 21:1-2, Genesis 30:22-23, 1 Samuel 1, Judges 13:2-3 and Luke 1:7, 25. Each birth was also a step in the story of salvation, for Isaac, Samuel and John the Baptist all had roles in God's plan. The picture is taken further by Isaiah 54:1, which Paul applies to the church: 'more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband,' Galatians 4:27. The correspondence reaches its height in Mary, who bore a child by the power of God. The type falls short in that these were gifts of a child, and the greater fruitfulness of the people of God is a work of the Spirit.

typology.type: The God who is high and bends low, verses 5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's prophecy that the high and holy One would dwell with the humble, Isaiah 57:15, is the pattern for the psalm's picture of a God who stoops. In the incarnation the stooping becomes literal: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, and the Son 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. On the night of the Passover He wrapped a towel around His waist and washed the disciples' feet, John 13:3-5. The correspondence is that the exalted one humbles Himself. The earlier pictures could only describe the stooping, while the incarnation is the stooping itself.

typology.type: The name praised from the sunrise to its setting, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The psalm looks to a day when the name of the LORD is honoured everywhere, and Malachi promised that His name would be great among the nations 'from where the sun rises to where it sets,' Malachi 1:11. The risen Christ, who has 'all authority in heaven and on earth,' sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:18-19, and John sees 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9. The escalation is from a hope to a mission and then to a vision. The pattern is not complete, for the praise of the nations is still being gathered.

study.christ:
The psalm describes a God who is highest and who stoops, and the New Testament sees that pattern in Jesus. Paul's hymn in Philippians 2 tells the same story in the same order. Christ, 'existing in the form of God,' did not grasp at equality with God, 'but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' and 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:6-8. Then 'God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names,' Philippians 2:9. The psalm's two movements, down and then up, are here found in one person. The name that the psalm wants praised from the rising of the sun to its setting is the name before which 'every knee should bow,' Philippians 2:10-11.

The reversal of verses 7 and 8 is the shape of His whole mission. He was born into poverty, laid in a feeding trough and first announced to shepherds, Luke 2:7-12. He told John's disciples that 'the good news is preached to the poor,' Luke 7:22, and said that He was among His followers 'as one who serves,' Luke 22:27. He taught that 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted,' Luke 14:11, and then lived it out. Going down into the dust of death, Psalm 22:15, He was raised and seated at God's right hand, and the psalm's phrase 'seat them with nobles' finds its meaning in the promise that those who are His are raised with Him and seated with Him in the heavenly realms, Ephesians 2:6.

The psalm's last scene, the barren woman who becomes a joyful mother, has its Christian form in the nativity story. Elizabeth, barren and old, is given a son, Luke 1:7 and 1:24-25, and Mary, a young woman of humble state, is told that she will bear the Son of God. Mary's song, Luke 1:46-55, is steeped in this psalm and in Hannah's prayer. 'He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant,' she says, and, 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' Luke 1:48, 52. The line of women who were lifted from shame leads to the one whose child lifts the whole world.

There is an extra weight if Jesus sang this psalm at the Last Supper. Matthew says that He and His disciples sang a hymn before they went out, Matthew 26:30, and the Hallel is the traditional song of the Passover meal. On the night He would be betrayed, the psalm on His lips described the thing He was about to do.

A caution about the limits: the psalm is a hymn to the LORD and does not predict the Messiah in any single line. The link to Christ rests on the pattern of the God it describes, and on the way the New Testament sees that God most clearly in His Son.
study.god:
This psalm gives one of the plainest statements in Scripture of what makes the LORD different from every rival. The question 'Who is like the LORD our God?' is answered by a pair of facts that no other god could claim at once. He is exalted above all the nations and above the heavens, and He bends down to look at the earth.

His transcendence is stated first and without any softening. He is 'exalted over all the nations, His glory above the heavens,' verse 4. His name is to be praised 'now and forevermore,' verse 2, and in every place from east to west, verse 3, so no region or period lies outside His claim. A God like this is not a tribal deity or a local power. Isaiah says that He sits above the circle of the earth and that its inhabitants are like grasshoppers, Isaiah 40:22. The psalm lets that stand and does not weaken it.

His nearness is not a contradiction of His height but a use of it. 'He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth,' verse 6, and even the heavens count as low to Him. The God who has to stoop to see the highest things stoops all the further for the lowest. His attention goes first to the people others ignore. The psalm names the poor, the needy and the barren woman, and each is a person without power, with no way to repay or to promote Himself. God's care for them is therefore not a reward for merit. Psalm 138:6 says that He attends to the lowly while the proud He knows from afar.

He is a God who reverses. The language of raising and seating shows that He is not content to leave the lowly where He finds them. He lifts them from the dust and sits them among the nobles of His people. In the same way He can bring joy where there was shame. Hannah sang that He brings death and gives life, that He humbles and exalts, 1 Samuel 2:6-7, and this psalm sings of the second half of each pair. God's sovereignty is here not only an exercise of power but of generosity.

He is a God to whom praise is due. The psalm begins and ends with Hallelujah, and the reason for the praise is given in the middle. It is not a general feeling of reverence but a response to what He is and does. A God who is both high and near deserves praise from servants, from nations and from every corner of the earth.

For worship, the psalm teaches that the right response to this God is both awe and ease. A believer may come with confidence into the presence of a God so great that heaven is beneath Him, because that same God takes notice of the poorest person in the room. And the worshipper who knows this will find it hard to look down on anyone.

crossReferences.note: Hannah's song, sung after the birth of Samuel, is the source of the psalm's central lines. Verse 8 matches verses 7 and 8 almost word for word, and verse 5 has the barren woman who bears seven.

Mary's Magnificat echoes both Hannah and this psalm. God looks on the humble state of His servant, brings down rulers and lifts the humble. The song shows the psalm being taken up as the voice of the coming of Christ.

The hymn of the Son who emptied Himself and was then exalted to the highest place is the psalm's pattern of high, low and high again, told of Christ. At His name every knee bows, as the psalm's name is praised in every place.
The high and lifted up One who inhabits eternity also dwells with the humble in spirit and revives the heart of the contrite. It states the same pairing of height and nearness as verses 5 and 6.
Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly, and the proud He knows from afar. It is a concise statement of what Psalm 113 sets out, and it adds that pride keeps God at a distance.

God's name will be great among the nations from where the sun rises to where it sets. Verse 3 of the psalm uses the same geography, and Malachi gives the hope that the whole world will one day join the praise.
The LORD attends to Sarah as He had promised, and she bears a son in old age. It is the first of the stories behind verse 9, in which a woman's long barrenness is ended by God's word.
Paul quotes Isaiah 54:1 about the barren woman and applies it to the free people of God, the children of promise. The psalm's final image of a joyful mother is widened to the whole church.
God made us alive with Christ and raised and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms. This is the fullest answer to the psalm's promise that He seats the poor from the dust among princes.

The suffering one says, 'You lay me in the dust of death.' The word for dust is the same that the psalm uses of the place from which God lifts the poor, so Christ goes into that place and brings His people out of it.
Jesus teaches that the one who exalts himself will be humbled and the one who humbles himself will be exalted. The reversal of the psalm is turned into a rule for life in the kingdom.

After the Passover meal Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn and went out. If the Hallel was sung, Psalm 113 was among its first songs, and the stooping God was praised on the night Jesus began the way of the cross.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God as high as He can be, speaking the heavens into being, and then immediately bending to shape a man from the dust of the ground and breathe life into him, Genesis 2:7. The psalm's two movements are already in the opening chapters. The fall, though, turned the dust into a sign of death, 'for dust you are, and to dust you will return,' Genesis 3:19, and much of what follows in the Old Testament is the story of God lifting people out of that dust.

It begins with a barren woman. Sarai 'was barren; she had no children,' Genesis 11:30, and the whole promise of the nations being blessed rested on a womb that could not bear. When God attended to Sarah, Genesis 21:1-2, the pattern of the psalm was set, and it recurs with Rachel, Hannah and the others. The nation itself is lifted from the dust of slavery in Egypt, and Psalm 114 follows this one to tell that story. Joseph rises from a dungeon, David from the sheepfold, and Hannah's son anoints the king. The exile throws Israel back into the dust, and Isaiah calls on Zion to 'shake off your dust' and 'sit on your throne,' Isaiah 52:2, in the language of the psalm.

Every one of these lifts is partial. The individuals were raised and then died, and the nation was restored and then fell again. The story is waiting for a lifting that does not fail. It comes in Jesus, who did what the psalm describes the LORD doing: He came down, took the form of a servant, went to the dust of death, and was exalted, Philippians 2:6-11. His resurrection is the great lifting from the dust. And because it is His, it becomes the lifting of all who belong to Him, who are raised and seated with Him, Ephesians 2:6.

The church is the barren woman who becomes the mother of many, Galatians 4:27, the people of promise made of the nations. They are gathered from every tribe and tongue, as the opening of the psalm hoped, from the rising of the sun to its setting, Revelation 5:9-10. These were once nobodies, and they are made 'a kingdom and priests' who will reign.

The new creation completes the psalm. 'The dwelling place of God is with man,' and the One who sits on the throne wipes every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:3-4. The God who is enthroned on high is also the God who lives among His people, and the dust, the ash heap and the barren home have all become places of joy. The Hallelujah that closes the psalm will never need to stop.

sermon.title: Grace and Glory
sermon.why: Keller works through Psalm 113:1-9 alongside the song of Hannah and the song of Mary, showing how the psalm's protocol, the infinitely high becoming inconceivably low, is worked out through Jesus Christ's own life, tending directly to this psalm's christological climax.

quiz.q: How wide is the geographic and temporal scope of the praise called for in verses 1-3?

options.text: From where the sun rises to where it sets, and both now and forevermore.
options.note: The praise called for spans every place and every time, a truly universal summons.

options.text: Only within the borders of Israel during festival seasons.
options.note: The text explicitly extends the call from sunrise to sunset, beyond any national border.

options.text: Only among the priesthood, never the general population.
options.note: The call addresses all servants of the LORD, not a restricted priestly class alone.

options.text: Only during a single specific historical event.
options.note: The language now and forevermore extends the call well beyond any single event.

quiz.q: What striking action does verse 6 attribute to the LORD despite His being enthroned on high?

options.text: He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth.
options.note: This stooping from the heights is the psalm's central turn toward God's condescending compassion.

options.text: He refuses to look upon the earth at all.
options.note: The verse says the opposite; He humbles Himself specifically to behold heaven and earth.

options.text: He delegates all earthly matters entirely to angels.
options.note: The text describes God's own personal stooping, not a delegation to intermediaries.

options.text: He remains distant and uninvolved with human affairs.
options.note: The whole point of the verse is God's active, personal involvement despite His transcendence.

quiz.q: According to verses 7-8, what does the LORD do for the poor and needy?

options.text: He raises them from the dust and seats them with nobles and princes.
options.note: This vivid reversal of status is the psalm's central picture of God's compassionate power.

options.text: He leaves them permanently in poverty as a test of character.
options.note: The text describes active lifting and honoring, not permanent abandonment in poverty.

options.text: He gives them wealth but withholds any social standing.
options.note: The text specifically says they are seated with princes, granting both honor and standing.

options.text: He requires them to lift themselves before He notices them.
options.note: The action described is entirely God's initiative, He raises and lifts them.

quiz.q: What Old Testament song does this psalm's language of raising the poor from the dust closely echo?

options.text: Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2:8.
options.note: Hannah's song uses nearly identical language of God lifting the poor and seating them with nobles.

options.text: The song of Moses at the Red Sea, Exodus 15.
options.note: That song celebrates deliverance from Egypt but does not share this specific dust and dunghill imagery.

options.text: The song of Deborah in Judges 5.
options.note: Deborah's song celebrates military victory, not this specific reversal-of-poverty imagery.

options.text: David's lament in 2 Samuel 1.
options.note: That is a lament over Saul and Jonathan's deaths, not a song of reversal for the poor.

quiz.q: How does Philippians 2:6-8 relate to this psalm's central theme?

options.text: It describes Christ's own stooping from divine glory to servanthood, the ultimate fulfillment of God's condescending love.
options.note: Christ's self-emptying embodies exactly the pattern of exaltation stooping to lowliness that this psalm celebrates.

options.text: It has no relationship to this psalm's themes.
options.note: Philippians 2 directly embodies this psalm's central movement of the exalted becoming lowly.

options.text: It describes only a future event with no present application.
options.note: Christ's incarnation described there is a past, historical event with ongoing present significance.

options.text: It focuses solely on physical poverty, unrelated to spiritual humility.
options.note: Philippians 2 focuses on Christ's spiritual and relational humility in taking on servanthood, not merely material poverty.

questions: This psalm calls for praise stretching from sunrise to sunset, every place and every hour. What would it look like for your own praise of God to become a rhythm through your whole day, not just a moment on Sunday?

God is described as stooping from His throne to notice the lowly. Where in your own life do you need to remember that God's greatness is shown not despite His attention to the small and overlooked, but precisely through it?

The psalm celebrates God raising the poor from the dust and seating them with princes. Who in your community is currently overlooked or without status, and how might you reflect God's character by honoring them?
The barren woman is given a joyful home. What situation in your life currently feels hopeless or barren, and how does this psalm's picture of God's reversing power speak into it?

Christ emptied Himself from the highest glory to become a servant and lift sinners from the dust of death. How does reflecting on His descent for you shape the way you respond to His call to serve others humbly this week?

translationNotes.note: Hallelujah transliterates the Hebrew Hallelu Yah, Praise the LORD, appearing at both the opening and closing of the psalm, verses 1 and 9, forming an inclusio that frames the whole hymn as praise.
Humbles Himself renders shaphel, a verb of stooping or bringing low, applied here to God's own gracious condescension to observe and act within heaven and earth.
The barren woman's home echoes the matriarchal narratives of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and especially Hannah, whose own song in 1 Samuel 2 shares this psalm's language of reversal almost word for word.
